title: Prehistory to Early Civilizations
description: Trace human history from early hominids through the first civilizations.
objectives: Describe human evolution and migration out of Africa
Explain the Neolithic Revolution's significance
Compare the first four river valley civilizations

lessons.title: Human Origins and Migration
lessons.content: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa ~300,000 years ago and spread across the globe.
examples: 'Out of Africa' model: all modern humans descend from African ancestors
By 12,000 BCE, humans had reached all continents except Antarctica
Megafauna extinction: humans likely drove mammoths, giant sloths, and other large animals extinct

title: Classical Civilizations
description: Analyze the classical civilizations of Greece, Rome, China, India, and the Americas.
objectives: Compare political systems of classical civilizations
Explain the Silk Road's role in cultural diffusion
Analyze causes of classical civilization collapse

lessons.title: Classical Political Systems
lessons.content: Classical civilizations developed a variety of governance models.
examples: Athens: direct democracy (limited to male citizens)
Rome: republic → empire; concept of citizenship
Han China: centralized empire governed by Confucian bureaucrats
Maurya Empire (India): centralized state; Ashoka adopted Buddhist ethics

title: Medieval and Early Modern World
description: Study the medieval world and the transitions to the early modern era.
objectives: Describe the rise and spread of Islam
Compare Medieval Europe with the Islamic world
Explain the significance of the Black Death

lessons.title: Rise of Islam
lessons.content: Islam arose in the Arabian Peninsula in the 7th century and spread rapidly.
examples: Muhammad received revelations from 610 CE; died 632 CE; had unified most of Arabia
Within 100 years of Muhammad's death, Muslim armies controlled from Spain to Central Asia
Five Pillars of Islam: Shahada, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj

lessons.title: The Black Death
lessons.content: The bubonic plague killed ~1/3 of Europe's population (1347–1353) — transforming medieval society.
examples: Spread along trade routes from Central Asia to Europe via Mongol trade networks
Killed ~25 million Europeans; labor shortage → peasants gained bargaining power
Undermined confidence in the Church; contributed to Renaissance questioning of tradition

title: Age of Exploration and Its Consequences
description: Analyze European exploration and its transformative — and often devastating — consequences.
objectives: Map major exploration routes
Analyze the Columbian Exchange in depth
Evaluate the demographic and cultural impact on the Americas

lessons.title: Exploration and Trade Routes
lessons.content: European exploration was driven by economic and religious motivations.
examples: Portugal: sought sea route to Asia to cut out Muslim middlemen; Vasco da Gama succeeded (1498)
Spain: Columbus (1492); Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided world between Spain and Portugal
England and France: sought northwest passage to Asia; colonized North America instead

lessons.title: Demographic Catastrophe
lessons.content: European contact caused the greatest demographic collapse in human history.
examples: Estimates vary: 50–90% of Indigenous American populations died within a century of contact
Disease (smallpox, measles, influenza) was the primary killer
Population of central Mexico fell from ~25 million in 1500 to ~1 million by 1600
This depopulation made large-scale African enslavement seem economically 'necessary' to colonizers

title: Revolutions — Political and Industrial
description: Examine the age of revolutions and how they reshaped political and economic life.
objectives: Analyze the intellectual origins of political revolution
Compare the American and French Revolutions
Explain the social impacts of industrialization

lessons.title: Political Revolutions
lessons.content: Enlightenment ideas challenged absolute monarchy and hereditary privilege.
examples: American Revolution (1776): first successful revolution based on Enlightenment principles
French Revolution (1789–1799): more radical; challenged religion, aristocracy, and monarchy; ended in Napoleon
Haitian Revolution (1791–1804): most radical of all — enslaved people won their freedom

lessons.title: Industrial Revolution's Social Impact
lessons.content: Industrialization created new social classes and enormous inequalities.
examples: Bourgeoisie (middle class): factory owners, professionals — gained power
Proletariat (working class): factory workers — long hours, dangerous conditions, low wages
Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto (1848) — predicted workers' revolution
Labor movement: strikes and unions → 8-hour workday, minimum wage, weekends

title: Imperialism and Nationalism
description: Study 19th-century imperialism and the rise of nationalism.
objectives: Explain economic and social motivations for imperialism
Describe nationalist movements
Analyze imperialism's legacy in the contemporary world

lessons.title: European Imperialism
lessons.content: European powers colonized most of the world in the 19th century.
examples: By 1914: Britain controlled 25% of Earth's land surface; France 9%
'White man's burden': racist ideology that justified colonialism as 'civilizing'
Resistance: Zulu Wars, Sepoy Mutiny, Boxer Rebellion — colonized peoples fought back

lessons.title: Nationalism
lessons.content: Nationalism — loyalty to a shared language/culture — both unified and destabilized nations.
examples: Italian unification (Risorgimento, 1861): Garibaldi and Cavour unified fragmented peninsula
German unification (1871): Bismarck used 'blood and iron' — wars and diplomacy
Nationalism in Austria-Hungary: multiple ethnic groups (Czechs, Slovaks, Serbs) wanted independence — leading to WWI

title: WWI and the Interwar Period
description: Examine WWI and the unstable interwar period that led to WWII.
objectives: Analyze WWI's causes in depth
Evaluate the Paris Peace Conference
Describe the rise of fascism

lessons.title: Paris Peace Conference
lessons.content: The 1919 Paris Peace Conference reshaped the world map but created new problems.
examples: Wilson's 14 Points: self-determination, League of Nations, no punitive peace — largely ignored
New nations created: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Iraq, Palestine (as British mandate)
Middle East mandate system: Britain and France divided Arab lands, ignoring promises made during the war

lessons.title: Rise of Fascism
lessons.content: Economic crisis and political instability produced fascist movements in Italy and Germany.
examples: Benito Mussolini: used black-shirted thugs to gain power in Italy (1922); glorified violence and the state
Adolf Hitler: blamed Germany's problems on Jews, communists, and 'foreign powers'; Hitler Youth indoctrination
Both regimes used propaganda, censorship, and terror to suppress opposition

title: WWII and the Holocaust
description: Study WWII in depth with special focus on the Holocaust and human rights.
objectives: Analyze WWII as a continuation of WWI's unresolved issues
Document the steps of the Holocaust
Evaluate post-war attempts at justice and human rights

lessons.title: Holocaust — Steps of Persecution
lessons.content: The Holocaust didn't begin with death camps — it was a step-by-step process.
examples: 1933–1938: legal discrimination; Jews stripped of citizenship (Nuremberg Laws, 1935)
1938: Kristallnacht ('Night of Broken Glass') — pogroms against Jewish homes and businesses
1941: mobile killing units (Einsatzgruppen) killed ~1 million Jews in Soviet territories
1942: Wannsee Conference — systematic plan for 'Final Solution' finalized

lessons.title: Post-War Justice
lessons.content: The world responded to the Holocaust with new institutions and legal frameworks.
examples: Nuremberg Trials (1945–46): 24 Nazi leaders tried for crimes against humanity — established international law precedent
Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948): proclaimed fundamental rights for all
State of Israel established (1948); United Nations created (1945)

title: Decolonization and Independence Movements
description: Examine the global wave of decolonization after WWII.
objectives: Explain why decolonization accelerated after WWII
Describe independence movements in India, Africa, and Southeast Asia
Evaluate the challenges of post-colonial nations

lessons.title: India's Independence
lessons.content: Gandhi's nonviolent independence movement inspired the world.
examples: Gandhi: satyagraha (nonviolent resistance); Salt March (1930) — walked 240 miles to protest British salt tax
WWII exhausted Britain economically and morally — empire became unsustainable
Independence (August 15, 1947): accompanied by Partition — India and Pakistan; ~15 million displaced; ~2 million died in violence

lessons.title: African Decolonization
lessons.content: Most of Africa gained independence between 1957 and 1975.
examples: Ghana (1957): first sub-Saharan African nation to gain independence; led by Kwame Nkrumah
Kenya: Mau Mau uprising (1952–60) combined with political pressure forced British withdrawal
Apartheid South Africa: remained white-minority ruled until Nelson Mandela's election (1994)

title: The Contemporary World
description: Analyze major developments shaping the contemporary world.
objectives: Describe the post-Cold War world
Analyze globalization and its effects
Evaluate major ongoing global challenges

lessons.title: Globalization
lessons.content: After 1991, the world became increasingly economically and culturally integrated.
examples: WTO, NAFTA, EU single market: reduced trade barriers
Global supply chains: your iPhone involves components from 43 countries
Cultural globalization: American films, K-pop, Bollywood reach global audiences

lessons.title: Current Global Challenges
lessons.content: The 21st century is defined by interconnected global challenges.
examples: Climate crisis: existential threat requiring global cooperation
Inequality: 1% of the world owns more than half of all wealth
Democracy under threat: authoritarian movements growing in many countries
Pandemic preparedness: COVID-19 revealed global vulnerabilities
